claim: Uromodulin is the most abundant protein in the urine.
source: Uromodulin is the most abundant protein in the urine.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction (Serafini-Cessi et al., 2003).

claim: Uromodulin is exclusively produced by renal epithelial cells.
source: It is exclusively produced by renal epithelial cells and it plays key roles in kidney function and disease.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the introduction describing exclusive expression in the kidney by epithelial cells lining the thick ascending limb (TAL) of Henle's loop.

claim: Uromodulin assembly depends on a conserved, specific proteolytic cleavage leading to conformational activation of a Zona Pellucida (ZP) polymerisation domain.
source: Uromodulin mainly exerts its function as an extracellular matrix whose assembly depends on a conserved, specific proteolytic cleavage leading to conformational activation of a Zona Pellucida (ZP) polymerisation domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Jovine et al., 2004; Schaeffer et al., 2009; Han et al., 2010).

claim: The membrane-bound serine protease hepsin is the enzyme responsible for the physiological cleavage of uromodulin.
source: Through a comprehensive approach, including extensive characterisation of uromodulin processing in cellular models and in specific knock-out mice, we demonstrate that the membrane-bound serine protease hepsin is the enzyme responsible for the physiological cleavage of uromodulin.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including cellular models, in vitro cleavage assays, and knockout mouse studies.

claim: Hepsin is the first in vivo substrate identified for this protease.
source: Our findings define a key aspect of uromodulin biology and identify the first in vivo substrate of hepsin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Uromodulin is a 105 kDa glycoprotein exclusively expressed in the kidney by epithelial cells lining the thick ascending limb (TAL) of Henle's loop.
source: Uromodulin, also known as Tamm-Horsfall protein, is a 105 kDa glycoprotein exclusively expressed in the kidney by epithelial cells lining the thick ascending limb (TAL) of Henle's loop.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about uromodulin.

claim: Uromodulin is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored protein mainly localised at the apical plasma membrane of TAL epithelial cells.
source: It is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored protein mainly localised at the apical plasma membrane of TAL epithelial cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about uromodulin.

claim: Uromodulin is secreted into the renal tubule through a conserved proteolytic cleavage.
source: Uromodulin is secreted into the renal tubule through a conserved proteolytic cleavage (Santambrogio et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: In the urine, uromodulin constitutes the most abundant protein under physiological conditions.
source: In the urine it constitutes the most abundant protein under physiological conditions (Serafini-Cessi et al., 2003) and it is mainly found as high molecular-weight polymers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Uromodulin polymerisation is mediated by its Zona Pellucida (ZP) domain.
source: Uromodulin polymerisation is mediated by its Zona Pellucida (ZP) domain, a module present in several proteins that assemble into extracellular polymers, such as components of the egg coat (including sperm receptors ZP3 and ZP2) and of the inner ear tectorial membrane (Jovine et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Specific cleavage is necessary for uromodulin assembly into polymers, as it releases an inhibitory hydrophobic motif (external hydrophobic patch, EHP) distal to the ZP domain that prevents polymerisation.
source: Specific cleavage is necessary for protein assembly into polymers, as it releases an inhibitory hydrophobic motif (external hydrophobic patch, EHP) distal to the ZP domain that prevents polymerisation (Jovine et al., 2004; Schaeffer et al., 2009; Han et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Uromodulin protects against urinary tract infections in Umod-/- mice.
source: Studies in Umod-/- mice demonstrated that it protects against urinary tract infections (Bates et al., 2004) and renal stone formation (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Uromodulin protects against renal stone formation in Umod-/- mice.
source: Studies in Umod-/- mice demonstrated that it protects against urinary tract infections (Bates et al., 2004) and renal stone formation (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Uromodulin modulates the activity of innate immunity cells via Toll-like receptor 4 signalling.
source: Uromodulin has also been shown to modulate the activity of innate immunity cells via Toll-like receptor 4 signalling (Säemann et al., 2005) or via activation of the inflammasome (Darisipudi et al., 2012) and to regulate granulopoiesis and systemic neutrophil homeostasis (Micanovic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Uromodulin modulates the activity of innate immunity cells via activation of the inflammasome.
source: Uromodulin has also been shown to modulate the activity of innate immunity cells via Toll-like receptor 4 signalling (Säemann et al., 2005) or via activation of the inflammasome (Darisipudi et al., 2012) and to regulate granulopoiesis and systemic neutrophil homeostasis (Micanovic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Uromodulin regulates granulopoiesis and systemic neutrophil homeostasis.
source: Uromodulin has also been shown to modulate the activity of innate immunity cells via Toll-like receptor 4 signalling (Säemann et al., 2005) or via activation of the inflammasome (Darisipudi et al., 2012) and to regulate granulopoiesis and systemic neutrophil homeostasis (Micanovic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Uromodulin is involved in the regulation of NaCl transport in the TAL by promoting surface expression of the renal outer medullary potassium channel (ROMK2).
source: Finally, it is involved in the regulation of NaCl transport in the TAL, based on its role in promoting surface expression of the renal outer medullary potassium channel (ROMK2) (Renigunta et al., 2011) and of the sodium-potassium-chloride co-transporter (NKCC2) (Mutig et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Uromodulin is involved in the regulation of NaCl transport in the TAL by promoting surface expression of the sodium-potassium-chloride co-transporter (NKCC2).
source: Finally, it is involved in the regulation of NaCl transport in the TAL, based on its role in promoting surface expression of the renal outer medullary potassium channel (ROMK2) (Renigunta et al., 2011) and of the sodium-potassium-chloride co-transporter (NKCC2) (Mutig et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Mutations in the uromodulin gene (UMOD) cause an autosomal dominant tubulo-interstitial kidney disease.
source: Mutations in the uromodulin gene (UMOD) cause an autosomal dominant tubulo-interstitial kidney disease (Hart, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Common variants in the UMOD gene are associated with increased risk for chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hypertension.
source: In addition, genome-wide association studies demonstrated that common variants in the UMOD gene are associated with increased risk for chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hypertension (Köttgen et al., 2009; Padmanabhan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The effect of UMOD variants on CKD and hypertension risk is due to higher UMOD expression driven by the presence of risk alleles in its gene promoter.
source: Such an effect is due to higher UMOD expression driven by the presence of risk alleles in its gene promoter (Trudu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Transfected human uromodulin assembles extracellularly in filamentous polymers in MDCK cells that are indistinguishable from urinary ones.
source: To understand the nature of such cleavage, we took advantage of a cellular system, Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) cells, where transfected human uromodulin assembles extracellularly in filamentous polymers (Figure 1B,C) that are indistinguishable from the urinary ones (Jovine et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citation and figures showing polymer formation.

claim: In MDCK cells, uromodulin is secreted as two isoforms that can be separated on gel electrophoresis after enzymatic removal of protein N-glycans at about 72 and 77 kDa.
source: In these cells, uromodulin is secreted as two isoforms that can be separated on gel electrophoresis after enzymatic removal of protein N-glycans at about 72 and 77 kDa (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1D.

claim: The longer uromodulin isoform is generated by a more distal cleavage and still retains the EHP.
source: while the longer one is generated by a more distal cleavage and still retains the EHP (Schaeffer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citation.

claim: The short uromodulin isoform released by MDCK cells corresponds to the one found in the urine, as it shares the same molecular weight and the same C-terminal residue (F587).
source: The short uromodulin isoform released by MDCK cells corresponds to the one found in the urine, as it shares the same molecular weight (Figure 1D) and the same C-terminal residue (F587 [Santambrogio et al., 2008]) (Figure 1E), demonstrating that uromodulin undergoes physiological cleavage in these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data (Figure 1D) and mass spectrometry data (Figure 1E), along with citation.

claim: Treatment with protease inhibitor cocktail (PIC) led to significant reduction of uromodulin polymerisation on the surface of MDCK cells.
source: This treatment led to significant reduction of uromodulin polymerisation on the surface of the cells (Figure 2A) that is not due to any alteration of protein expression or intracellular distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), confirming that the polymerisation-competent uromodulin isoform is generated through the action of a protease.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: Only inhibitors of serine proteases significantly reduced uromodulin polymerisation in MDCK cells.
source: We then treated MDCK cells with the single PIC components, each targeting a specific catalytic type of protease, and observed that only inhibitors of serine proteases significantly reduced uromodulin polymerisation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: Expression of the Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitor Hepatocyte growth factor Activator Inhibitor-1 (HAI-1) essentially abolished uromodulin polymerisation on the surface of MDCK cells.
source: Consistently, the expression of the Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitor Hepatocyte growth factor Activator Inhibitor-1 (HAI-1) (Shimomura et al., 1997) essentially abolished uromodulin polymerisation on the surface of MDCK cells and reduced the secretion of the shorter uromodulin isoform (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A soluble isoform of uromodulin (S614X) was neither processed to the shorter variant nor formed polymers in MDCK cells.
source: Interestingly, this isoform was neither processed to the shorter variant nor it formed polymers (Figure 2B,C), indicating that, as in the case of ZP3 (Jovine et al., 2002), membrane association is necessary to allow uromodulin physiological cleavage and polymerisation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Membrane association is necessary to allow uromodulin physiological cleavage and polymerisation.
source: Interestingly, this isoform was neither processed to the shorter variant nor it formed polymers (Figure 2B,C), indicating that, as in the case of ZP3 (Jovine et al., 2002), membrane association is necessary to allow uromodulin physiological cleavage and polymerisation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data from the soluble uromodulin mutant experiment.

claim: Physiological cleavage of uromodulin depends on a serine protease that is likely membrane associated.
source: From these results we conclude that physiological cleavage of uromodulin depends on a serine protease, and that this enzyme is likely membrane associated.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the protease inhibitor and membrane association experiments.

claim: Uromodulin expressed in HEK293 cells did not form polymers on the cell surface.
source: We moved further starting from the interesting observation that uromodulin expressed in a different kidney-derived cell line, Human Embryonic Kidney 293 (HEK293), did not form polymers on the cell surface (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A.

claim: Only the longer polymerisation-incompetent uromodulin isoform was released by HEK293 cells.
source: Accordingly, only the longer polymerisation-incompetent uromodulin isoform was released by these cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data in Figure 3B.

claim: Four candidate enzymes were identified through transcriptome comparison: prostasin (Prss8), hepsin/TMPRSS1 (Hpn), mucin 1 (Muc1) and dipeptidyl-peptidase IV (Dpp4).
source: This strategy led to the identification of only four candidate enzymes: prostasin (Prss8), hepsin/TMPRSS1 (Hpn), mucin 1 (Muc1) and dipeptidyl-peptidase IV (Dpp4) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the selection process shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Dpp4 and Muc1 were excluded as candidates based on their catalytic activity.
source: The last two enzymes were excluded on the basis of their catalytic activity: Dpp4 sequentially removes N-terminal dipeptides from polypeptides, cleaving after a proline residue (Mentlein, 1999), whereas Muc1 contains a self-cleaving module rather than a classical peptidase S1 domain (Levitin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: Both hepsin and prostasin are inhibited by the Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitor HAI-1.
source: Interestingly, both proteases are inhibited by the Kunitz-type serine protease inhibitor HAI-1 (Fan et al., 2005; Herter et al., 2005), in line with our results in MDCK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: Expression of wild-type hepsin or prostasin in HEK293 cells induced short cleavage and polymerisation of uromodulin.
source: We validated our hypothesis by expressing either hepsin or prostasin in HEK293 cells. This induced short cleavage as well as polymerisation of uromodulin, an effect that was dependent on the catalytic activity of the enzymes, as it was abolished when catalytically inactive isoforms of the proteases were expressed (Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The effect of hepsin and prostasin on uromodulin cleavage is dependent on the catalytic activity of the enzymes.
source: This induced short cleavage as well as polymerisation of uromodulin, an effect that was dependent on the catalytic activity of the enzymes, as it was abolished when catalytically inactive isoforms of the proteases were expressed (Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data comparing wild-type and catalytically inactive proteases.

claim: Both hepsin and prostasin could be specifically co-immunoprecipitated with uromodulin from the lysates of HEK293 cells.
source: Moreover, this effect is likely direct, as both enzymes could be specifically co-immunoprecipitated with uromodulin from the lysates of HEK293 cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3F.

claim: Both hepsin and prostasin induced a mass shift of efUmod and loss of its C-terminal histidine tag when incubated with purified efUmod.
source: When incubated with purified efUmod, both hepsin and prostasin induced a mass shift of efUmod as well as loss of its C-terminal histidine tag (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in vitro cleavage assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: The effects of hepsin and prostasin on efUmod were abolished by mutagenesis of the consensus cleavage site.
source: These effects were abolished by mutagenesis of the consensus cleavage site (efUmod YAla, carrying the mutation 586RFRS589 > 586AYAA589).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in vitro cleavage assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: Hepsin was more efficient than prostasin at cleaving uromodulin, as it completely digested the substrate despite being used at lower concentration.
source: Interestingly, hepsin was more efficient than prostasin, since it completely digested the substrate despite being used at lower concentration (see figure legend).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by in vitro cleavage assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: Transfected hepsin and prostasin both co-localised with uromodulin on the apical membrane of polarised MDCK cells.
source: Indeed, while endogenous proteases could not be detected, possibly because of low expression levels or low affinity for the employed antibodies (which were raised against their human counterparts), transfected hepsin and prostasin both co-localised with uromodulin on the apical membrane of polarised MDCK cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by confocal immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A.

claim: Only hepsin silencing led to a significant reduction of uromodulin polymerisation on the cell surface of MDCK cells.
source: We successfully obtained comparable expression knock-down for both enzymes (Figure 5B), but only hepsin silencing led to a significant reduction of uromodulin polymerisation on the cell surface (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Real-Time qPCR data (Figure 5B) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 5C).

claim: Hepsin is the enzyme responsible for uromodulin cleavage at the urinary site in MDCK cells.
source: These results demonstrate that hepsin is the enzyme responsible for uromodulin cleavage at the urinary site in MDCK cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the silencing experiments.

claim: Strong hepsin expression was detected in the TAL of mouse kidneys.
source: Remarkably, by microdissecting mouse nephron segments, we detected strong hepsin expression in the TAL (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Real-Time qPCR data on microdissected nephron segments in Figure 6A.

claim: Hepsin co-localises with uromodulin on the apical membrane of TAL epithelial cells in mouse kidneys.
source: Moreover, hepsin co-localises with uromodulin on the apical membrane of TAL epithelial cells, suggesting a functional interaction between the two proteins (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6B.

claim: Urinary uromodulin levels were significantly reduced in Hpn-/- mice.
source: Notably, urinary uromodulin levels were significantly reduced in Hpn-/- mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data in Figure 6C.

claim: Reduced urinary uromodulin in Hpn-/- mice was accompanied by marked accumulation of the mature, fully glycosylated form of uromodulin in kidney lysates.
source: This was accompanied by marked accumulation of the mature, fully glycosylated form of uromodulin in kidney lysates (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data in Figure 6D.

claim: No difference was observed in the cellular distribution of uromodulin in TAL cells of Hpn-/- mice, showing typical apical membrane enrichment.
source: On the other hand, no difference was observed in the cellular distribution of uromodulin in TAL cells, showing typical apical membrane enrichment (Figure 6E), and no change in Umod gene expression was detected (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6E.

claim: No change in Umod gene expression was detected in Hpn-/- mice.
source: On the other hand, no difference was observed in the cellular distribution of uromodulin in TAL cells, showing typical apical membrane enrichment (Figure 6E), and no change in Umod gene expression was detected (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Real-Time qPCR data in Figure 6F.

claim: Reduced levels of urinary uromodulin in Hpn-/- mice are due to defective protein secretion rather than changes in protein expression or transport to the apical plasma membrane.
source: These data exclude that reduced levels of urinary uromodulin in Hpn-/- mice could be due to changes in protein expression or transport to the apical plasma membrane, strongly suggesting defective protein secretion.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the data from Hpn-/- mice.

claim: Urinary uromodulin from Hpn-/- mice appeared as two isoforms after deglycosylation: a short one with similar electrophoretic mobility as in wild-type urines, and a longer one normally undetectable in urines from wild-type mice.
source: After deglycosylation, urinary uromodulin from Hpn-/- mice appeared as two isoforms: a short one, with similar electrophoretic mobility as in wild-type urines, and a longer one, normally undetectable in urines from wild-type mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data in Figure 7A.

claim: The short uromodulin isoform from Hpn-/- mice lacks the physiological C-terminus (F588) and is produced by a more distal cleavage occurring after residue R607.
source: Mass-spectrometry analysis on the short isoform showed that it lacks the physiological C-terminus (F588) and is produced by a more distal cleavage occurring after residue R607 (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 7B-D.

claim: The long uromodulin isoform from Hpn-/- mice has a C-terminus after residue K616.
source: The same analysis on the long isoform revealed an even more distal C-terminus, after residue K616 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), consistent with its slower electrophoretic mobility.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Absence of hepsin abolishes uromodulin cleavage at the physiological site and induces its misprocessing.
source: These data demonstrate that absence of hepsin abolishes uromodulin cleavage at the physiological site and induces its misprocessing.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the mass spectrometry data from Hpn-/- mice.

claim: Uromodulin from Hpn-/- urines was not sedimented in the pellet fraction of a biochemical polymerisation assay, indicating that the residual urinary protein is not assembled into polymers.
source: Interestingly, uromodulin from Hpn-/- urines was not sedimented in the pellet fraction of a biochemical polymerisation assay (Jovine et al., 2002) (Figure 7E), indicating that the residual urinary protein is not assembled into polymers.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by polymerisation assay data in Figure 7E.

claim: Both urinary uromodulin isoforms in Hpn-/- mice are misprocessed and still retain the polymerisation-inhibiting EHP motif.
source: This is consistent with the observation that both urinary isoforms in Hpn-/- mice are misprocessed and still retain the polymerisation-inhibiting EHP motif (Figure 7D) (Jovine et al., 2004; Schaeffer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the mass spectrometry data showing cleavage sites distal to the EHP.

claim: Weak prostasin expression was detected in TAL segments where it co-localises with uromodulin on the apical plasma membrane of epithelial cells.
source: Confirming data from available transcriptomes, we detected weak prostasin expression in TAL segments where it co-localises with uromodulin on the apical plasma membrane of epithelial cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Real-Time qPCR and immunofluorescence data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Secretion of urinary uromodulin in Prss8-/- mice was comparable to controls.
source: We then generated an adult nephron-specific Prss8-/- mouse model and analysed urinary uromodulin. Secretion of urinary uromodulin in these mice was comparable to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Urinary uromodulin from Prss8-/- mice shares the same C-terminal residue as control animals.
source: Moreover, mass-spectrometry analysis on the urinary protein confirmed that it shares the same C-terminal residue of control animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E,F), excluding a role for prostasin in uromodulin processing in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: Prostasin does not play a role in uromodulin processing in vivo.
source: Moreover, mass-spectrometry analysis on the urinary protein confirmed that it shares the same C-terminal residue of control animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E,F), excluding a role for prostasin in uromodulin processing in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the data from Prss8-/- mice.

claim: Hepsin is the enzyme responsible for the physiological release of uromodulin in the urine.
source: Collectively, our results identify hepsin as the enzyme responsible for the physiological release of uromodulin in the urine.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion section based on all the experimental findings.

claim: The identification of hepsin as the enzyme responsible for uromodulin release reveals an important biological function of this type II transmembrane serine protease in the renal epithelium.
source: By identifying hepsin as the enzyme responsible for the release of uromodulin in the renal tubule, our results reveal an important biological function of this type II transmembrane serine protease in the renal epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Lack of hepsin does not affect baseline renal function of Hpn-/- mice.
source: Lack of hepsin does not affect baseline renal function of Hpn-/- mice (serum creatinine: wild-type 0.78 +/- 0.04 vs Hpn-/- 0.74 +/- 0.14 mg/dL, n = 5/group, p=0.59; blood urea nitrogen: wild-type 21.6 +/- 3.29 vs Hpn-/- 20.8 +/- 4.12 mg/dL, n= 5/group, p=0.76).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen measurements.

claim: Hepsin-mediated cleavage likely takes place at the plasma membrane where the two proteins co-localise.
source: Considering the maturation steps of uromodulin along the secretory compartment, hepsin-mediated cleavage likely takes place at the plasma membrane where the two proteins co-localise, allowing the protein to traffic within the cell in a polymerisation-incompetent conformation, and to polymerise only once it is secreted (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an interpretation based on the co-localisation data and the model shown in Figure 8.

claim: The C-terminus of human and mouse urinary uromodulin has been mapped to a phenylalanine residue (F587 and F588, respectively).
source: Interestingly, the C-terminus of human and mouse urinary uromodulin has been mapped to a phenylalanine residue (F587 and F588, respectively) (Santambrogio et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: Hepsin preferentially cleaves substrates after basic amino acids.
source: Since in vitro studies showed that hepsin preferentially cleaves substrates after basic amino acids (Herter et al., 2005; Béliveau et al., 2009; Owen et al., 2010), this could result from cleavage at the following arginine residue and subsequent C-terminal trimming.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Post-cleavage trimming by carboxypeptidases has been proposed for several secreted proteins, including urokinase and ZP subunits.
source: Post-cleavage trimming by carboxypeptidases is not uncommon and it has already been proposed for several secreted proteins, including urokinase (Günzlerwa et al., 1982), and ZP subunits (Kubo et al., 1999; Boja et al., 2003; Darie et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Hepsin is the first protease involved in the physiological cleavage of a ZP domain protein.
source: Through the identification of hepsin as the protease releasing uromodulin in the urine we discover the first protease involved in the physiological cleavage of a ZP domain protein, which is a pre-requisite for polymerisation of this type of molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Hpn-/- mice were reported to have profound hearing loss likely due to inner ear defects, including a deformed and enlarged tectorial membrane.
source: Notably, Hpn-/- mice were reported to have profound hearing loss likely due to inner ear defects, including a deformed and enlarged tectorial membrane (Guipponi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: The tectorial membrane consists of filaments largely composed of ZP domain proteins α- and β-tectorin.
source: This acellular structure, which overlays the organ of Corti, consists of filaments largely composed of ZP domain proteins α- and β-tectorin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: The morphology of the tectorial membrane is similarly altered in mice carrying deafness-causing mutations in α-tectorin that are likely affecting protein secretion.
source: The morphology of the tectorial membrane is similarly altered in mice carrying deafness-causing mutations in α-tectorin (Legan et al., 2014) that are likely affecting protein secretion (Jovine et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Inner ear tectorins are likely physiological substrates of hepsin.
source: These findings, along with data presented in this manuscript, suggest that inner ear tectorins are also physiological substrates of hepsin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculation based on the findings and literature.

claim: Release of glycoprotein-2, a ZP domain protein highly homologous to uromodulin that is predominantly expressed in pancreas, is mediated by an apical protease sensitive to serine protease inhibitors.
source: Moreover, release of glycoprotein-2, a ZP domain protein highly homologous to uromodulin that is predominantly expressed in pancreas, is mediated by an apical protease sensitive to serine protease inhibitors (Fritz and Lowe, 1996), again suggesting the involvement of hepsin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citation.

claim: The results identifying hepsin as the protease cleaving uromodulin are likely relevant for other members of the ZP domain protein family.
source: In light of these observations and given the conserved function of the ZP domain and the high similarity of the consensus cleavage site of ZP domain proteins (Jovine et al., 2004), our results are likely to be relevant for other members of this protein family.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculation based on the findings and the conserved nature of ZP domains.
